Chapter 8: Building Influence and Leading Change
When you think about leadership, what comes to mind? Is it holding a certain title, or having the final say? The truth is, real leadership isn’t just about authority—it’s about influence. It’s your ability to shape outcomes, inspire the people around you, and spark positive change.
Influence doesn’t happen overnight. It’s something you build, step by step, by showing credibility, forming strong relationships, and having a sense of purpose that others can rally behind. When you act with integrity, keep your promises, and communicate a vision that excites, your influence naturally grows.
But there’s more to it than just speaking up. It’s about really listening—getting to know what matters to others, understanding what drives them, and finding those shared goals that bring people together.
So, how can you start building your own influence? Here are a few practical steps that make a real difference:
First, develop your expertise. Become that go-to person—the one others trust for advice in your field.
Next, invest in relationships. Spend time getting to know your colleagues, stakeholders, and everyone on your team. Those connections are your foundation.
Communicate your vision and values. Don’t just focus on what needs to be done—share why it matters. People are drawn to purpose.
Support others’ success, too. Whether you’re mentoring, advocating, or simply celebrating team wins, you’re building trust and goodwill.
And don’t forget about organizational politics. Navigate those informal networks with integrity—use them to push for positive goals, not personal gain.
Now, let’s talk about leading change. That’s where influence really comes to life. Leading change takes vision and—let’s be honest—a lot of persistence. Change can make people anxious. There’s often resistance, whether from fear, uncertainty, or just competing interests.
The best leaders see these challenges coming. They tackle them with empathy and clarity, making space for honest conversations.
Imagine you’re rolling out a new workflow at work. You’d start by explaining why this change matters, then really listen to any concerns. You’d get the team involved in shaping how things will look—and you’d find those informal influencers, the folks everyone respects, to help build momentum.
Here’s something important: real influence isn’t about manipulating people or promoting yourself. It’s about creating alignment—a sense of shared purpose that everyone can get behind.
And for women, building influence sometimes means pushing back against old power structures, and speaking up for more inclusive, collaborative ways of working.
So, if you want to lead change, start by building trust, staying true to your values, and inviting others to shape the journey with you. That’s how real influence—and real progress—takes root.
